Hierarchical Kernel Transformer: Multi-Scale Attention with an Information-Theoretic Approximation Analysis

Giansalvo Cirrincione giansalvo.cirrincione@u-picardie.fr organization=Laboratoire LTI, Université de Picardie Jules Verne, addressline=33 rue Saint-Leu, city=Amiens, postcode=80039, country=France
Abstract

The self-attention mechanism at the core of modern Transformer models treats every pair of tokens in a sequence with equal architectural capacity, regardless of how far apart they are. This single-scale bias limits performance on tasks that require reasoning simultaneously at short and long range, while incurring quadratic computational cost in sequence length.

The Hierarchical Kernel Transformer (HKT) is proposed, a multi-scale attention mechanism that processes the input sequence at multiple resolution levels simultaneously. At each level, a compressed version of the sequence is obtained by trainable causal downsampling; attention scores are computed independently at each level and combined through learned weights. This design captures both local patterns and long-range structure with a total computational cost of at most 4/34/3 times that of standard attention, regardless of the number of levels (1.3125×1.3125\times for three levels).

Four theoretical contributions are established: (i) the hierarchical scoring function defines a positive semidefinite kernel under a sufficient condition on the symmetrised bilinear form (Proposition 3.1); (ii) the asymmetric score matrix decomposes uniquely into a symmetric component controlling reciprocal attention and an antisymmetric component controlling directional attention, with HKT providing LL independent such pairs across scales (Propositions 3.5–3.6); (iii) the approximation error decomposes into three interpretable components with an explicit non-Gaussian correction and a geometric decay bound in the number of levels (Theorem 4.3, Proposition 4.4); (iv) HKT strictly subsumes standard attention and causal convolution in the single-head setting (Proposition 3.4).

Empirically, HKT achieves consistent gains over retrained standard attention baselines across three tasks of different modalities (mean ±\pm std, 3 seeds): +4.77+4.77pp on synthetic ListOps (55.10±0.29%55.10\pm 0.29\% vs 50.33±0.12%50.33\pm 0.12\%, T=512T=512), +1.44+1.44pp on sequential CIFAR-10 (35.45±0.09%35.45\pm 0.09\% vs 34.01±0.19%34.01\pm 0.19\%, T=1,024T=1{,}024), and +7.47+7.47pp on IMDB character-level sentiment classification (70.19±0.57%70.19\pm 0.57\% vs 62.72±0.40%62.72\pm 0.40\%, T=1,024T=1{,}024), all at 1.31×1.31\times computational overhead.

1 Introduction

The self-attention mechanism (Vaswani et al., 2017) has become the dominant computational primitive in sequence modelling. For a sequence of TT tokens, attention computes a weighted average of value vectors, where the weights are determined by pairwise dot products between query and key projections. This single operation, repeated across layers, has proven remarkably expressive across a wide range of tasks.

Yet this simplicity conceals a structural limitation. Standard self-attention is scale-blind: a token at position tt attends to every other token with the same architectural capacity, whether the target is adjacent or at distance T/2T/2. The network must learn to ignore distant tokens when local context suffices, and to attend globally when long-range reasoning is required, with no structural prior to guide either regime.

This limitation becomes critical on long-sequence tasks. The Long Range Arena (LRA) benchmark (Tay et al., 2021) systematically documents this failure: standard MHA achieves only 36.37%36.37\% on ListOps at sequence length T=2,048T=2{,}048. Efficient attention variants (Beltagy et al., 2020; Choromanski et al., 2021) address computational cost but not the structural bias: they restrict which pairs are computed, not how multi-scale structure is captured.

A different approach is taken here. Rather than sparsifying or approximating the attention matrix, it is factored across scales. The Hierarchical Kernel Transformer (HKT) computes attention at LL resolution levels, with each level operating on a downsampled representation of the sequence. The level-ll score matrix captures interactions at scale sls^{l}, where s≥2s\geq 2 is the downsampling stride. The final attention is a learned convex combination of level-specific scores, upsampled to the original resolution.

This design has three properties that standard attention lacks. First, it is structurally multi-scale: level ll captures the frequency band [π/sl,π/sl−1][\pi/s^{l},\pi/s^{l-1}] in the sequence spectrum (Proposition 3.3). Second, it is computationally efficient: the total cost is 43​(1−4−L)\frac{4}{3}(1-4^{-L}) times MHA, bounded above by 43\frac{4}{3} regardless of LL (Proposition 4.6). Third, it admits information-theoretic guarantees: the approximation error per hierarchical level is bounded in terms of the mutual information I⁡(S(l),f⁡(X))I(S^{(l)};f(X)), related explicitly to the squared multiple correlation ρl2\rho_{l}^{2} and the non-Gaussianity index κl\kappa_{l} (Theorem 4.3).

Contributions.

The following contributions are made:

  1. 1.

    Architecture (Section 3). HKT is defined as a hierarchical attention mechanism combining LL resolution levels with a hybrid conv/attention head and input-dependent level fusion.

  2. 2.

    Kernel theory (Section 3). The hierarchical score matrix is shown to define a PSD kernel under a sufficient condition on the symmetrised bilinear form (Proposition 3.1), its Gram matrix factorises as a sum of per-level PSD matrices with an explicit rank bound (Proposition 3.2), and HKT is shown to strictly subsume single-head attention and causal convolution in the single-layer, H=1H=1 setting (Proposition 3.4).

  3. 3.

    Asymmetric score analysis (Section 3.6). A direct analysis of the asymmetric score function used in practice is provided, without symmetrisation. The symmetric-antisymmetric decomposition M(l)=Ms(l)+Ma(l)M^{(l)}=M_{s}^{(l)}+M_{a}^{(l)} is shown to separate reciprocity (mutual attention strength, controlled by Ms(l)M_{s}^{(l)}) from directionality (attention asymmetry, controlled by Ma(l)M_{a}^{(l)}) (Proposition 3.5, Corollary 3.7). HKT with LL levels disposes of LL independent such pairs, one per scale (Proposition 3.6). This analysis applies to the operational model and explains why the PSD condition is not satisfied in trained models.

  4. 4.

    Approximation theory (Section 4). A three-term error decomposition is derived with an explicit non-Gaussian bound on the information-theoretic reduction per level, presented as a motivated approximation framework extending the Gaussian process results of Roberts et al. (2022) to finite-width networks.

  5. 5.

    Experiments (Section 5). Consistent improvements over retrained MHA baselines are obtained on two tasks: +4.7+4.7pp on synthetic ListOps (T=512T=512) and +1.98+1.98pp on sequential CIFAR-10 (T=1,024T=1{,}024), both at 1.31×1.31\times computational overhead. Sensitivity analysis across L∈{1,2,3,4}L\in\{1,2,3,4\} and s∈{2,3}s\in\{2,3\} confirms that the gains are robust to hyperparameter choice.

2 Related Work

Efficient attention.

A large body of work reduces the 𝒪⁡(T2)\mathcal{O}(T^{2}) cost of attention through sparsity (Beltagy et al., 2020; Zaheer et al., 2020), low-rank approximation (Wang et al., 2020; Choromanski et al., 2021), or linear kernels (Katharopoulos et al., 2020). These methods address computational cost without introducing hierarchical structure. HKT is orthogonal: hierarchical structure is added at bounded additional cost rather than reducing existing capacity.

Hierarchical and multi-scale transformers.

Hierarchical processing is central to convolutional networks (LeCun et al., 1998) and has been incorporated into vision transformers through patch-merging windows (Liu et al., 2021a), pooling-based token compression (Liu et al., 2021b), and cluster-based token merging (Wang et al., 2021). These methods operate on spatial data and downsample hidden states rather than attention scores. More recently, FasterViT (Hatamizadeh et al., 2024) decomposes global self-attention into local window attention and hierarchical carrier tokens, achieving competitive accuracy-throughput trade-offs on image classification. HAT-Net (Liu et al., 2024) proposes hierarchical MHSA that computes local attention first and then models global dependencies on merged tokens. Both FasterViT and HAT-Net target vision tasks and reduce computational cost by restricting attention scope; HKT instead constructs independent score matrices at each resolution and fuses them with learned weights, maintaining full expressivity at each scale while bounding total cost.

Hierarchical transformers for sequences.

For text, hierarchical transformers exploit document structure (words →\to sentences →\to sections) to handle long inputs efficiently. HDT (He et al., 2024) processes long documents by interleaving local and global attention in a single layer using an efficient hierarchical attention pattern. HIBRIDS (Cao and Wang, 2022) introduces hierarchical biases for structure-aware long document summarisation. These methods rely on explicit structural segmentation of the input. HKT instead learns a continuous multi-scale decomposition via causal downsampling, making no assumptions about document structure and extending naturally to non-textual sequences.

State space models.

Structured state space models (SSMs) such as Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2023) offer an alternative to attention for long-sequence modelling, achieving linear time complexity via selective state propagation. Mamba achieves strong results on the LRA benchmark and matches or exceeds transformers of similar size on language tasks. HKT and Mamba address different aspects of the long-sequence problem: Mamba replaces attention with a recurrent mechanism, while HKT retains the attention mechanism and augments it with explicit multi-scale structure. The two approaches are complementary and could in principle be combined (multi-scale Mamba layers with hierarchical state updates), which we leave as future work.

Kernel methods for attention.

The connection between attention and kernel methods has been formalised in Tsai et al. (2019); Katharopoulos et al. (2020); Choromanski et al. (2021). Performers (Choromanski et al., 2021) approximate the softmax kernel with random feature maps. HKT employs a sum of hierarchical kernels, each PSD under a sufficient condition (Proposition 3.1), without approximation. The asymmetric score decomposition M(l)=Ms(l)+Ma(l)M^{(l)}=M_{s}^{(l)}+M_{a}^{(l)} (Section 3.6) provides a direct analysis of the operational model that complements the kernel-theoretic view.

Long Range Arena.

Tay et al. (2021) introduced LRA as a systematic benchmark for long-range sequence models, comprising five tasks with sequence lengths up to 4,0964{,}096. On ListOps, standard MHA achieves 36.37%36.37\%, Longformer 35.63%35.63\%, and Performer 18.01%18.01\%. The synthetic variant used here reproduces the algebraic structure of ListOps at T=512T=512.

Gaussian process limits.

Roberts et al. (2022) establish that sufficiently wide networks converge to Gaussian processes, with corrections of order 𝒪⁡(1/d)\mathcal{O}(1/d). Lemma 4.2 extends this analysis to the information content of hierarchical score matrices, providing an explicit non-Gaussian correction for the finite-width regime.

At level l∈{0,…,L−1}l\in\{0,\ldots,L-1\}:

Tl\displaystyle T_{l} ≔⌊T/sl⌋(sequence length at level l),\displaystyle\coloneqq\lfloor T/s^{l}\rfloor\quad\text{(sequence length at level }l\text{)},
dl\displaystyle d_{l} ≔max(d/2l, 32)(embedding dimension at level l),\displaystyle\coloneqq\max(d/2^{l},\,32)\quad\text{(embedding dimension at level }l\text{)},

By convention, X(0)≔XX^{(0)}\coloneqq X, T0=TT_{0}=T, d0=dd_{0}=d. The learnable weight matrices are: WQ(l),WK(l)∈ℝdk(l)×dlW_{Q}^{(l)},W_{K}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}^{(l)}\times d_{l}} (query and key projections at level ll); WV(l)∈ℝd×dlW_{V}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{l}} (value projection); WO(l)∈ℝd×dW_{O}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} (output projection); γ∈ℝL\gamma\in\mathbb{R}^{L} (fusion weight logits), giving λl≔softmax​(γ)l\lambda_{l}\coloneqq\mathrm{softmax}(\gamma)_{l}; γ~∈ℝH×L\tilde{\gamma}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times L} (hybrid mixing logits), giving βh(l)≔σ⁡(γ~h​l)∈(0,1)\beta_{h}^{(l)}\coloneqq\sigma(\tilde{\gamma}_{hl})\in(0,1).

3.2 Hierarchical kernel scoring

Level-ll representations.

For l≥1l\geq 1, the level-ll representation X(l)∈ℝTl×dlX^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{T_{l}\times d_{l}} is:

X(l)=ϕl∘⋯∘ϕ1(X(0)),X^{(l)}=\phi_{l}\circ\cdots\circ\phi_{1}(X^{(0)}), (1)

where each ϕl′:ℝTl′−1×dl′−1→ℝTl′×dl′\phi_{l^{\prime}}:\mathbb{R}^{T_{l^{\prime}-1}\times d_{l^{\prime}-1}}\to\mathbb{R}^{T_{l^{\prime}}\times d_{l^{\prime}}} is a depthwise-separable causal convolution (kernel size k=3k=3, stride ss) followed by LayerNorm and GELU activation. Left-padding with k−1k-1 zeros enforces causality: [X(l)]m[X^{(l)}]_{m} depends only on [X(l−1)]0,…,[X(l−1)]m​s[X^{(l-1)}]_{0},\ldots,[X^{(l-1)}]_{ms}.

Si​j(l)=⟨WQ(l)​Xi(l),WK(l)​Xj(l)⟩dk(l),i,j∈{0,…,Tl−1}.S^{(l)}_{ij}=\frac{\langle W_{Q}^{(l)}X^{(l)}_{i},\;W_{K}^{(l)}X^{(l)}_{j}\rangle}{\sqrt{d_{k}^{(l)}}},\quad i,j\in\{0,\ldots,T_{l}-1\}. (2)

Si​jhier=∑l=0L−1λl⋅S~⌊i/sl⌋,⌊j/sl⌋(l),i,j∈{0,…,T−1},S^{\mathrm{hier}}_{ij}=\sum_{l=0}^{L-1}\lambda_{l}\cdot\tilde{S}^{(l)}_{\lfloor i/s^{l}\rfloor,\;\lfloor j/s^{l}\rfloor},\quad i,j\in\{0,\ldots,T-1\}, (3)

Proposition 3.1 (Hierarchical kernel is PSD under a sufficient condition).

Define the symmetrised level-ll matrix M(l)≔(WQ(l)⊤​WK(l)+WK(l)⊤​WQ(l))/(2​dk(l))M^{(l)}\coloneqq(W_{Q}^{(l)\top}W_{K}^{(l)}+W_{K}^{(l)\top}W_{Q}^{(l)})/(2\sqrt{d_{k}^{(l)}}) and the associated kernel

klsym​(x,y)≔exp⁡(x⊤​M(l)​y).k_{l}^{\mathrm{sym}}(x,y)\coloneqq\exp\!\left(x^{\top}M^{(l)}y\right). (4)

If M(l)M^{(l)} is positive semidefinite, then klsymk_{l}^{\mathrm{sym}} is a PSD kernel, and Khiersym​(Xi,Xj)≔∑l=0L−1λl​klsym​(X⌊i/sl⌋(l),X⌊j/sl⌋(l))K_{\mathrm{hier}}^{\mathrm{sym}}(X_{i},X_{j})\coloneqq\sum_{l=0}^{L-1}\lambda_{l}k_{l}^{\mathrm{sym}}(X^{(l)}_{\lfloor i/s^{l}\rfloor},X^{(l)}_{\lfloor j/s^{l}\rfloor}) is PSD for any λl≥0\lambda_{l}\geq 0.

Proof.

When M(l)⪰0M^{(l)}\succeq 0, the function k⁡(x,y)=exp⁡(x⊤​M(l)​y)k(x,y)=\exp(x^{\top}M^{(l)}y) is PSD because it equals the inner product ⟨ϕ⁡(x),ϕ⁡(y)⟩\langle\phi(x),\phi(y)\rangle in the feature space induced by the Taylor expansion of the exponential, where each monomial OPENx⊤​M(l)​y)n/n!x^{\top}M^{(l)}y)^{n}/n! corresponds to a PSD kernel (product of a PSD kernel is PSD by closure). A non-negative linear combination of PSD kernels is PSD.

Remark on the PSD condition. M(l)M^{(l)} is symmetric by construction but not necessarily PSD, since WQ(l)⊤​WK(l)W_{Q}^{(l)\top}W_{K}^{(l)} may have negative eigenvalues. The condition M(l)⪰0M^{(l)}\succeq 0 can be enforced by initialisation (e.g. WQ(l)=WK(l)W_{Q}^{(l)}=W_{K}^{(l)}) or by projecting M(l)M^{(l)} onto the PSD cone after each gradient step. In practice, neither constraint is imposed. We verified empirically that the PSD condition is not satisfied by trained models: across all 12 configurations (4 encoder layers ×\times 3 hierarchy levels) of a trained HKT-Small, approximately 50%50\% of eigenvalues of M(l)M^{(l)} are negative (min eigenvalue ranging from −0.51-0.51 to −0.08-0.08). This is consistent with M(l)M^{(l)} being a generic symmetric matrix: without an explicit PSD constraint, gradient descent has no reason to confine M(l)M^{(l)} to the PSD cone. The symmetrised kernel therefore serves as a theoretical surrogate rather than a description of the actual trained model (see Definition 1 below). ∎

Definition 1 (Practical note on asymmetric scores).

In practice, WQ(l)≠WK(l)W_{Q}^{(l)}\neq W_{K}^{(l)} and the raw score Si​j(l)=⟨WQ(l)​xi,WK(l)​xj⟩/dk(l)S^{(l)}_{ij}=\langle W_{Q}^{(l)}x_{i},W_{K}^{(l)}x_{j}\rangle/\sqrt{d_{k}^{(l)}} is not symmetric. The symmetrised kernel klsymk_{l}^{\mathrm{sym}} of Proposition 3.1 is therefore a theoretical surrogate: it establishes that the scoring mechanism is close to a PSD kernel (specifically, that the symmetric part of the bilinear form x⊤​M(l)​yx^{\top}M^{(l)}y is PSD), while the asymmetric component encodes the directional query–key distinction that is essential for expressivity in practice. The gap between theory and implementation is deliberate and analogous to the standard treatment of asymmetric attention in kernel attention literature (Tsai et al., 2019; Choromanski et al., 2021): the symmetric surrogate provides geometric structure, the asymmetric model provides flexibility. Closing this gap formally — proving a PSD result directly for the asymmetric score — would require either restricting WQ=WKW_{Q}=W_{K} (standard kernel attention) or adopting a non-symmetric positive definite framework, both of which reduce expressivity.

Let Φ(l)∈ℝN×dl\Phi^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{l}} denote the matrix whose ii-th row is xi(l)x_{i}^{(l)}, the level-ll compressed representation of sample ii. Define ψ(l):ℝdl→ℋ(l)\psi^{(l)}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{l}}\to\mathcal{H}^{(l)} as the Mercer feature map of klsymk_{l}^{\mathrm{sym}}, and let Ψ(l)∈ℋ(l)​N\Psi^{(l)}\in\mathcal{H}^{(l)N} be the matrix whose ii-th row is ψ(l)​(xi(l))\psi^{(l)}(x_{i}^{(l)}). Then the Gram matrix 𝐊hier∈ℝN×N\mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{hier}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N} admits the factorisation:

𝐊hier=∑l=0L−1λl​Ψ(l)​Ψ(l)⊤,\mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{hier}}=\sum_{l=0}^{L-1}\lambda_{l}\,\Psi^{(l)}\Psi^{(l)\top}, (5)

where each term λl​Ψ(l)​Ψ(l)⊤\lambda_{l}\Psi^{(l)}\Psi^{(l)\top} is PSD. Two consequences follow:

  1. (i)

    Rank bound: rank⁡(𝐊hier)≤∑l=0L−1min⁡(N, 2​dk(l))\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{hier}})\leq\sum_{l=0}^{L-1}\min(N,\,2d_{k}^{(l)}).

  2. (ii)

    Local co-occurrence bias: two tokens xi,xjx_{i},x_{j} sharing the same compressed block at level ll (i.e. xi(l)=xj(l)x_{i}^{(l)}=x_{j}^{(l)}) receive the maximum level-ll kernel value, creating a multi-scale preference for locally co-occurring token pairs.

See Appendix A for the complete proof.

Proof.

By definition, [𝐊(l)]i​j=klsym​(xi(l),xj(l))=⟨ψ(l)​(xi(l)),ψ(l)​(xj(l))⟩ℋ(l)[\mathbf{K}^{(l)}]_{ij}=k_{l}^{\mathrm{sym}}(x_{i}^{(l)},x_{j}^{(l)})=\langle\psi^{(l)}(x_{i}^{(l)}),\psi^{(l)}(x_{j}^{(l)})\rangle_{\mathcal{H}^{(l)}}, so 𝐊(l)=Ψ(l)​Ψ(l)⊤\mathbf{K}^{(l)}=\Psi^{(l)}\Psi^{(l)\top}. This is PSD as a Gram matrix. Summing with non-negative weights gives (5).

(i) Rank bound (finite-dimensional approximation). Strictly speaking, the RKHS ℋ(l)\mathcal{H}^{(l)} of the exponential kernel klsymk_{l}^{\mathrm{sym}} is infinite-dimensional, so dimℋ(l)=∞\dim\mathcal{H}^{(l)}=\infty and rank⁡(𝐊(l))≤N\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{K}^{(l)})\leq N trivially. The bound rank⁡(𝐊(l))≤2​dk(l)\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{K}^{(l)})\leq 2d_{k}^{(l)} holds under the practical approximation that only the linear term of the Taylor expansion of exp⁡(⋅)\exp(\cdot) is retained (i.e. the kernel is approximated by its first-order feature map ϕ⁡(x)=WQ(l)​x\phi(x)=W_{Q}^{(l)}x and WK(l)​xW_{K}^{(l)}x), which has dimension 2​dk(l)2d_{k}^{(l)}. This approximation is standard in the kernel attention literature (Tsai et al., 2019; Choromanski et al., 2021) and reflects the effective rank of attention matrices in practice, but it is not a tight bound on the exact RKHS dimension.

(ii) If xi(l)=xj(l)=:vx_{i}^{(l)}=x_{j}^{(l)}=:v, then klsym​(v,v)=exp⁡(v⊤​M(l)​v/dk(l))k_{l}^{\mathrm{sym}}(v,v)=\exp(v^{\top}M^{(l)}v/\sqrt{d_{k}^{(l)}}), which is the maximum of klsym​(⋅,⋅)k_{l}^{\mathrm{sym}}(\cdot,\cdot) at that point by positive definiteness of the exponentiated form. ∎

3.4 Frequency-domain interpretation (heuristic)

Proposition 3.3 (Heuristic spectral interpretation).

Under the approximations of weakly stationary inputs and ideal low-pass downsampling filters (approximately satisfied for kernel size k=3k=3, stride s=2s=2):

𝔼X​[klsym​(Xm(l),Xm′(l))]≈Cl⋅exp⁡(1σl2​∫π/slπ/sl−1R^​(ω)​cos⁡(ω⁡(m−m′)​sl)​𝑑ω),\mathbb{E}_{X}\!\left[k_{l}^{\mathrm{sym}}\!\left(X^{(l)}_{m},X^{(l)}_{m^{\prime}}\right)\right]\approx C_{l}\cdot\exp\!\left(\frac{1}{\sigma_{l}^{2}}\int_{\pi/s^{l}}^{\pi/s^{l-1}}\hat{R}(\omega)\cos\!\left(\omega(m-m^{\prime})s^{l}\right)d\omega\right),

where R^​(ω)\hat{R}(\omega) is the input spectral density, Cl>0C_{l}>0 a normalisation constant, and σl>0\sigma_{l}>0 the bandwidth parameter of klsymk_{l}^{\mathrm{sym}}. Level ll thus preferentially captures sequence content in the band [π/sl,π/sl−1][\pi/s^{l},\pi/s^{l-1}]. This is a motivating interpretation, not a rigorous result. See Appendix B for derivation.

3.5 Representational capacity

Let ℱattn​(H,d,T)\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{attn}}(H,d,T) denote the class of functions computable by a single-layer MHA with HH heads, embedding dimension dd, and sequence length TT, and let ℱconv​(d,k)\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{conv}}(d,k) denote those computable by causal depthwise convolution with kernel size kk and dimension dd. Let ℱHKT​(H,d,L,s,T)\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{HKT}}(H,d,L,s,T) denote the corresponding HKT class with LL levels and stride ss.

Proposition 3.4 (Representational capacity).

In the setting H≥1H\geq 1, d≥2d\geq 2, T≥4T\geq 4, L≥2L\geq 2, s=2s=2:

  1. (i)

    (Inclusion) ℱattn​(H,d,T)⊆ℱHKT​(H,d,L,s,T)\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{attn}}(H,d,T)\subseteq\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{HKT}}(H,d,L,s,T) and ℱconv​(d,k)⊆ℱHKT​(H,d,L,s,T)\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{conv}}(d,k)\subseteq\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{HKT}}(H,d,L,s,T).

  2. (ii)

    (Strict inclusion for H=1H=1) There exists a function f∈ℱHKT​(1,d,L,s,T)∖(ℱattn​(1,d,T)∪ℱconv​(d,k))f\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{HKT}}(1,d,L,s,T)\setminus(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{attn}}(1,d,T)\cup\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{conv}}(d,k)).

For H≥2H\geq 2, HKT strictly subsumes the single-scale (L=1L=1) variant and causal convolution by construction, but whether it strictly subsumes general HH-head MHA depends on the expressivity of multi-head composition and is left as an open question.

Proof.

(i) Setting βh(l)=1\beta_{h}^{(l)}=1, λ0=1\lambda_{0}=1, λl=0\lambda_{l}=0 for l≥1l\geq 1 reduces HKT to standard MHA. Setting βh(l)=0\beta_{h}^{(l)}=0 for all h,lh,l reduces it to causal depthwise convolution.

(ii) Restrict to H=1H=1, T=4T=4, s=2s=2, L=2L=2. Consider the witness function f⁡(X)=⟨x0,x2⟩+⟨x0,x1⟩f(X)=\langle x_{0},x_{2}\rangle+\langle x_{0},x_{1}\rangle, where xi∈ℝdx_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Not in ℱconv\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{conv}}: Causal depthwise convolution with kernel size kk computes outt=∑j=0k−1Wj⊙xt−j\mathrm{out}_{t}=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}W_{j}\odot x_{t-j}, which is linear in XX. The function ff is degree-2 bilinear, hence f∉ℱconv​(d,k)f\notin\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{conv}}(d,k).

Not in ℱattn​(1,d,T)\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{attn}}(1,d,T): A single-head attention at position 00 computes out0=∑j=0T−1aj​(X)⋅WV​xj\mathrm{out}_{0}=\sum_{j=0}^{T-1}a_{j}(X)\cdot W_{V}x_{j} where aj​(X)=softmax​(⟨WQ​x0,WK​xj⟩/dk)ja_{j}(X)=\mathrm{softmax}(\langle W_{Q}x_{0},W_{K}x_{j}\rangle/\sqrt{d_{k}})_{j}. The output is linear in WV​XW_{V}X, with scalar attention weights aja_{j}. For ff to be representable, one would need ∑jaj​WV​xj=W∗​x1⋅⟨u,x0⟩+W∗⁣∗​x2⋅⟨v,x0⟩\sum_{j}a_{j}W_{V}x_{j}=W^{*}x_{1}\cdot\langle u,x_{0}\rangle+W^{**}x_{2}\cdot\langle v,x_{0}\rangle for some fixed u,v,W∗,W∗⁣∗u,v,W^{*},W^{**}, which requires the attention weights to simultaneously encode two independent inner products. Since aja_{j} depends only on the ratio ⟨WQ​x0,WK​xj⟩\langle W_{Q}x_{0},W_{K}x_{j}\rangle, this cannot be achieved for generic x0,x1,x2x_{0},x_{1},x_{2} with a single head. (A complete formal proof requires a characterisation of the function class of single-head attention, which we leave as a precise technical claim rather than a closed theorem.)

In ℱHKT​(1,d,2,2,4)\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{HKT}}(1,d,2,2,4): At level l=0l=0, the score S01(0)S^{(0)}_{01} captures ⟨x0,x1⟩\langle x_{0},x_{1}\rangle. After downsampling with s=2s=2, the compressed pair at level l=1l=1 represents (x0,x2)(x_{0},x_{2}), so S00(1)S^{(1)}_{00} captures ⟨x0,x2⟩\langle x_{0},x_{2}\rangle. With fusion weights λ0=λ1=1/2\lambda_{0}=\lambda_{1}=1/2, the hierarchical score ShierS^{\mathrm{hier}} encodes both interactions simultaneously. ∎

3.6 Asymmetric score analysis via symmetric-antisymmetric decomposition

The PSD analysis of the preceding sections applies to a symmetrised surrogate kernel. This section develops a complementary analysis that applies directly to the asymmetric score function used in practice, without any symmetrisation.

Setup.

At level ll, the score matrix is S(l)=X(l)​M(l)​X(l)⊤/dk(l)S^{(l)}=X^{(l)}M^{(l)}X^{(l)\top}/\sqrt{d_{k}^{(l)}} where M(l)=WQ(l)⊤​WK(l)∈ℝdl×dlM^{(l)}=W_{Q}^{(l)\top}W_{K}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{l}\times d_{l}} is a general (non-symmetric) matrix. Every square matrix admits a unique decomposition:

M(l)=Ms(l)+Ma(l),M^{(l)}=M_{s}^{(l)}+M_{a}^{(l)}, (8)

where Ms(l)≔(M(l)+M(l)⊤)/2M_{s}^{(l)}\coloneqq(M^{(l)}+M^{(l)\top})/2 is symmetric and Ma(l)≔(M(l)−M(l)⊤)/2M_{a}^{(l)}\coloneqq(M^{(l)}-M^{(l)\top})/2 is antisymmetric (Ma(l)⊤=−Ma(l)M_{a}^{(l)\top}=-M_{a}^{(l)}).

Proposition 3.5 (Reciprocity-Directionality Identity).

For any two positions i,j∈{0,…,Tl−1}i,j\in\{0,\ldots,T_{l}-1\}:

Si​j(l)+Sj​i(l)\displaystyle S^{(l)}_{ij}+S^{(l)}_{ji} =2dk(l)​xi(l)⊤​Ms(l)​xj(l),\displaystyle=\frac{2}{\sqrt{d_{k}^{(l)}}}x_{i}^{(l)\top}M_{s}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}, (9)
Si​j(l)−Sj​i(l)\displaystyle S^{(l)}_{ij}-S^{(l)}_{ji} =2dk(l)​xi(l)⊤​Ma(l)​xj(l).\displaystyle=\frac{2}{\sqrt{d_{k}^{(l)}}}x_{i}^{(l)\top}M_{a}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}. (10)

Consequently:

  1. (i)

    (Reciprocity) Ma(l)=0M_{a}^{(l)}=0 if and only if Si​j(l)=Sj​i(l)S^{(l)}_{ij}=S^{(l)}_{ji} for all i,j,X(l)i,j,X^{(l)} (attention is symmetric).

  2. (ii)

    (Directionality) Ms(l)=0M_{s}^{(l)}=0 if and only if Si​j(l)=−Sj​i(l)S^{(l)}_{ij}=-S^{(l)}_{ji} for all i,j,X(l)i,j,X^{(l)} (attention is purely antisymmetric).

  3. (iii)

    Ms(l)M_{s}^{(l)} controls how much token ii and token jj mutually attend to each other; Ma(l)M_{a}^{(l)} controls the direction of the attention asymmetry.

Proof.

Direct computation: Si​j(l)+Sj​i(l)=(xi⊤​M​xj+xj⊤​M​xi)/dk=xi⊤​(M+M⊤)​xj/dk=2​xi⊤​Ms​xj/dkS^{(l)}_{ij}+S^{(l)}_{ji}=(x_{i}^{\top}Mx_{j}+x_{j}^{\top}Mx_{i})/\sqrt{d_{k}}=x_{i}^{\top}(M+M^{\top})x_{j}/\sqrt{d_{k}}=2x_{i}^{\top}M_{s}x_{j}/\sqrt{d_{k}}. The antisymmetric identity follows analogously. Parts (i)–(iii) follow immediately from (9) and (10) and the fact that x⊤​A​x=0x^{\top}Ax=0 for all xx iff AA is antisymmetric. ∎

Proposition 3.6 (Scale separation).

Let T≥sL−1+1T\geq s^{L-1}+1 and let 𝒜l\mathcal{A}_{l} denote the set of attention matrices producible by a single-level model operating on X(l)X^{(l)} with parameter matrix M∈ℝdl×dlM\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{l}\times d_{l}}:

𝒜l≔{softmax⁡(X(l)​M​X(l)⊤dk(l))|M∈ℝdl×dl}.\mathcal{A}_{l}\coloneqq\Bigl\{\mathrm{softmax}\!\Bigl(\frac{X^{(l)}MX^{(l)\top}}{\sqrt{d_{k}^{(l)}}}\Bigr)\;\Big|\;M\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{l}\times d_{l}}\Bigr\}.

For l≠l′l\neq l^{\prime}, the sets 𝒜l\mathcal{A}_{l} and 𝒜l′\mathcal{A}_{l^{\prime}} operate on representations of different lengths (Tl=⌊T/sl⌋≠Tl′=⌊T/sl′⌋T_{l}=\lfloor T/s^{l}\rfloor\neq T_{l^{\prime}}=\lfloor T/s^{l^{\prime}}\rfloor) and are therefore incommensurable: no single attention matrix on X(0)X^{(0)} can reproduce the score structure of a model operating on X(l)X^{(l)} for l≥1l\geq 1, since the downsampled representations X(l)X^{(l)} are nonlinear functions of X(0)X^{(0)} obtained through the causal downsampling cascade (1).

Consequently, HKT’s hierarchical score Shier=∑lλl↑lS(l)S^{\mathrm{hier}}=\sum_{l}\lambda_{l}\uparrow_{l}S^{(l)} (where ↑l\uparrow_{l} denotes upsampling to length TT) lies outside the convex hull of 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} for generic inputs and generic non-zero λ1,…,λL−1\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{L-1}.

Proof.

The representations X(l)X^{(l)} for l≥1l\geq 1 are obtained by applying the causal depthwise-separable convolution cascade ϕl∘⋯∘ϕ1\phi_{l}\circ\cdots\circ\phi_{1} to X(0)X^{(0)} (equation (1)). Each ϕl′\phi_{l^{\prime}} applies a strided convolution followed by LayerNorm and GELU, which is a nonlinear map. The composite map X(0)↦X(l)X^{(0)}\mapsto X^{(l)} is therefore nonlinear for l≥1l\geq 1.

Fix l≥1l\geq 1 and suppose for contradiction that there exists M~∈ℝd0×d0\tilde{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}\times d_{0}} such that X(0)M~X(0)⊤=c⋅↑l(X(l)M(l)X(l)⊤)X^{(0)}\tilde{M}X^{(0)\top}=c\cdot\uparrow_{l}(X^{(l)}M^{(l)}X^{(l)\top}) for all X(0)∈ℝT×d0X^{(0)}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_{0}} and some c>0c>0. The left side is a degree-2 polynomial in the entries of X(0)X^{(0)}. The right side involves X(l)=fl​(X(0))X^{(l)}=f_{l}(X^{(0)}) where flf_{l} is nonlinear (contains GELU), so the right side is not a degree-2 polynomial in X(0)X^{(0)} for generic M(l)M^{(l)}. This is a contradiction, completing the proof. ∎

Corollary 3.7 (Directional energy decomposition).

Define the directional energy at level ll as:

𝒟(l)≔∑i≠j(Si​j(l)−Sj​i(l))2=4dk(l)​∑i≠j(xi(l)⊤​Ma(l)​xj(l))2.\mathcal{D}^{(l)}\coloneqq\sum_{i\neq j}\bigl(S^{(l)}_{ij}-S^{(l)}_{ji}\bigr)^{2}=\frac{4}{d_{k}^{(l)}}\sum_{i\neq j}\bigl(x_{i}^{(l)\top}M_{a}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}\bigr)^{2}. (11)

Then 𝒟(l)=0\mathcal{D}^{(l)}=0 for all inputs X(l)X^{(l)} if and only if Ma(l)=0M_{a}^{(l)}=0.

Proof.

The equality in (11) follows directly from Proposition 3.5 (10). If Ma(l)=0M_{a}^{(l)}=0 then every term vanishes. Conversely, if Ma(l)≠0M_{a}^{(l)}\neq 0, there exist vectors u,v∈ℝdlu,v\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{l}} with u⊤​Ma(l)​v≠0u^{\top}M_{a}^{(l)}v\neq 0 (since Ma(l)≠0M_{a}^{(l)}\neq 0 as a linear map). Setting xi(l)=ux_{i}^{(l)}=u and xj(l)=vx_{j}^{(l)}=v for some i≠ji\neq j gives a strictly positive contribution to 𝒟(l)\mathcal{D}^{(l)}. ∎

Remark 1 (Connection to the empirical PSD failure).

The empirical finding that Ms(l)M_{s}^{(l)} is not PSD for any trained configuration (Section 6) is not explained by Ma(l)≠0M_{a}^{(l)}\neq 0 alone — the two facts are logically independent (a matrix can have Ma≠0M_{a}\neq 0 and still have Ms⪰0M_{s}\succeq 0, as the example M=(2102)M=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\ 0&2\end{pmatrix} shows). The PSD failure is instead a consequence of the unconstrained optimisation: gradient descent has no objective that would confine Ms(l)M_{s}^{(l)} to the PSD cone. The directional energy analysis and the PSD analysis are therefore complementary, not redundant: Corollary 3.7 characterises the asymmetric component; Proposition 3.1 characterises a constrained variant in which the symmetric component would be PSD.

Implication for HKT.

Proposition 3.5 shows that the asymmetric attention mechanism of HKT is not a defect of the PSD surrogate analysis but a structural feature: Ma(l)≠0M_{a}^{(l)}\neq 0 is what allows the model to represent directed relationships (token ii queries token jj differently from how jj queries ii). Proposition 3.6 shows that HKT amplifies this capacity: with LL levels, it can represent LL independent directional patterns, each at a different spatial scale. This is a direct theoretical result about the operational model, not about a symmetrised surrogate.

4 Approximation Theory

This section establishes theoretical guarantees for HKT. Let N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} denote the number of training samples and ℋK\mathcal{H}_{K} the reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) associated with KhierK_{\mathrm{hier}} — the function space in which HKT operates. The following assumptions are made throughout.

Assumption 1 (H1 – RKHS membership).

The target function f∈ℋKf\in\mathcal{H}_{K}, with ‖f‖ℋK≤B<∞\|f\|_{\mathcal{H}_{K}}\leq B<\infty.

Assumption 2 (H2 – Lipschitz and finite kurtosis).

Each klk_{l} is LlL_{l}-Lipschitz in its first argument. The normalised Mardia kurtosis κl\kappa_{l} (defined below) satisfies κl<∞\kappa_{l}<\infty.

Assumption 3 (H3 – i.i.d. training data).

The model is trained on NN i.i.d. samples from 𝒟\mathcal{D}.

Lemma 4.1 (Lipschitz bound on KhierK_{\mathrm{hier}}).

Under Assumption 2, for δ≔maxi⁡‖Xi−Xi′‖2\delta\coloneqq\max_{i}\|X_{i}-X^{\prime}_{i}\|_{2}:

|Khier​(Xi,Xj)−Khier​(Xi′,Xj)|≤δ​∑l=0L−1λl​Ll​∏m=0l−1‖Wdown(m)‖op,|K_{\mathrm{hier}}(X_{i},X_{j})-K_{\mathrm{hier}}(X^{\prime}_{i},X_{j})|\leq\delta\sum_{l=0}^{L-1}\lambda_{l}L_{l}\prod_{m=0}^{l-1}\|W_{\mathrm{down}}^{(m)}\|_{\mathrm{op}},

where Wdown(m)W_{\mathrm{down}}^{(m)} is the weight of ϕm\phi_{m}.

Lemma 4.2 (Non-Gaussian information bound).

Let ρl2∈[0,1)\rho_{l}^{2}\in[0,1) be the squared multiple correlation coefficient of f⁡(X)f(X) regressed on S(l)S^{(l)}, estimated via Ridge regression on the PCA-projected features. Define the normalised Mardia kurtosis (Mardia, 1970) of the joint distribution of (S(l),f⁡(X))(S^{(l)},f(X)) projected to pp principal components:

κl≔b2,p(l)p⁡(p+2),b2,p(l)≔1N​∑i,jdi​j2,\kappa_{l}\coloneqq\frac{b_{2,p}^{(l)}}{p(p+2)},\quad b_{2,p}^{(l)}\coloneqq\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i,j}d_{ij}^{2}, (12)

where di​jd_{ij} is the sample Mahalanobis distance.

(Motivated approximation.) Under the approximation that the conditional entropy h⁡(f⁡(X)∣S(l))h(f(X)\mid S^{(l)}) is lower-bounded by its Gaussian value, and applying the maximum-entropy bound for distributions with finite kurtosis (Cover and Thomas, 2006) to the marginal h⁡(f⁡(X))h(f(X)):

I⁡(S(l),f⁡(X))≲−12​log⁡(1−ρl2)+κl−12​ρl2+𝒪⁡(κl2N).I\!\left(S^{(l)};\,f(X)\right)\;\lesssim\;-\tfrac{1}{2}\log(1-\rho_{l}^{2})+\frac{\kappa_{l}-1}{2}\,\rho_{l}^{2}+\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\kappa_{l}^{2}}{N}\right). (13)

The approximation is exact under joint Gaussianity (κl=1\kappa_{l}=1, Assumption H2’), reducing to I⁡(S(l),f⁡(X))=−12​log⁡(1−ρl2)I(S^{(l)};f(X))=-\tfrac{1}{2}\log(1-\rho_{l}^{2}). The term (κl−1)​ρl2/2(\kappa_{l}-1)\rho_{l}^{2}/2 quantifies the non-Gaussian correction; Experiment 3 (Section 5.7) shows κl≈33\kappa_{l}\approx 33 for trained models at d≤512d\leq 512, making this correction dominant in practice.

Derivation sketch.

Decompose I=h⁡(f⁡(X))−h⁡(f⁡(X)∣S(l))I=h(f(X))-h(f(X)\mid S^{(l)}). Apply the maximum-entropy bound h⁡(Y)≤12​log⁡(2​π​e​σ2)+(κ−1)​σ2/2+𝒪⁡(κ2/N)h(Y)\leq\tfrac{1}{2}\log(2\pi e\sigma^{2})+(\kappa-1)\sigma^{2}/2+\mathcal{O}(\kappa^{2}/N) (Cover and Thomas, 2006) to h⁡(f⁡(X))h(f(X)). Lower-bound h⁡(f⁡(X)∣S(l))h(f(X)\mid S^{(l)}) by its Gaussian value 12​log⁡(2​π​e​σf2​(1−ρl2))\tfrac{1}{2}\log(2\pi e\sigma_{f}^{2}(1-\rho_{l}^{2})) (this step is exact under H2’ and an approximation otherwise). Combining gives (13). ∎

Theorem 4.3 (HKT Approximation Framework).

Under Assumptions 1–3, and the motivated approximation of Lemma 4.2, the L2​(μ)L^{2}(\mu) approximation error satisfies:

‖f−f^‖L2​(μ)≤ε0−∑l=1L−1λl​Δlng⏟εhier+Cβ​CL​supi‖Xi−X^i‖2⏟εquant+𝒪⁡(BN)⏟εopt,\|f-\hat{f}\|_{L^{2}(\mu)}\leq\underbrace{\varepsilon_{0}-\sum_{l=1}^{L-1}\lambda_{l}\Delta_{l}^{\mathrm{ng}}}_{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{hier}}}+\underbrace{C_{\beta}C_{L}\sup_{i}\|X_{i}-\hat{X}_{i}\|_{2}}_{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{quant}}}+\underbrace{\mathcal{O}\!\left(\tfrac{B}{\sqrt{N}}\right)}_{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{opt}}}, (14)

where the three terms represent the hierarchical approximation error (how well LL scales cover the target function), the quantisation error (information lost by downsampling), and the optimisation error (finite-sample learning). The constants are: B≔‖f‖ℋKB\coloneqq\|f\|_{\mathcal{H}_{K}} (RKHS norm of the target, finite by Assumption H1); σf2≔Var⁡(f⁡(X))\sigma_{f}^{2}\coloneqq\mathrm{Var}(f(X)) (target variance); ρ02≔0\rho_{0}^{2}\coloneqq 0 (no information at level −1-1, by convention); ε0≔εapprox(0)\varepsilon_{0}\coloneqq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{approx}}^{(0)} (approximation error of flat, single-scale attention); Δlng≔[σf2​(ρl2−ρl−12)−(κl−1)​ρl2]/(2​ε0)\Delta_{l}^{\mathrm{ng}}\coloneqq\bigl[\sigma_{f}^{2}(\rho_{l}^{2}-\rho_{l-1}^{2})-(\kappa_{l}-1)\rho_{l}^{2}\bigr]/(2\varepsilon_{0}) is the net error reduction at level ll: the first term is the information gain from adding level ll, the second is the non-Gaussian penalty; Δlng\Delta_{l}^{\mathrm{ng}} can be negative when the penalty exceeds the gain, in which case level ll should receive weight λl=0\lambda_{l}=0; Cβ≔(∑lλl​‖Wdown(l)‖op2)1/2C_{\beta}\coloneqq\bigl(\sum_{l}\lambda_{l}\|W_{\mathrm{down}}^{(l)}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}\bigr)^{1/2} (aggregate Lipschitz constant of the downsampling cascade); CL≔(∑lλl​Ll2)1/2C_{L}\coloneqq\bigl(\sum_{l}\lambda_{l}L_{l}^{2}\bigr)^{1/2} (weighted kernel Lipschitz constant); X^i\hat{X}_{i} is the reconstructed token representation after downsampling and upsampling at level ll, so ‖Xi−X^i‖2\|X_{i}-\hat{X}_{i}\|_{2} measures distortion introduced by lossy compression.

Corollary 4.4 (Optimal level weights).

The weight λl∗\lambda_{l}^{*} maximising Δlng\Delta_{l}^{\mathrm{ng}} per unit cost Cl=𝒪⁡(Tl2)C_{l}=\mathcal{O}(T_{l}^{2}) satisfies λl∗∝(ρl2−ρl−12−(κl−1)​ρl2)/Cl\lambda_{l}^{*}\propto(\rho_{l}^{2}-\rho_{l-1}^{2}-(\kappa_{l}-1)\rho_{l}^{2})/C_{l}. In the near-Gaussian regime (κl≈1\kappa_{l}\approx 1): λl∗∝s−l\lambda_{l}^{*}\propto s^{-l}.

Proposition 4.5 (Error decay with depth).

Define the residual error after ll levels as εl≔ε0−∑l′=1lλl′​Δl′ng\varepsilon_{l}\coloneqq\varepsilon_{0}-\sum_{l^{\prime}=1}^{l}\lambda_{l^{\prime}}\Delta_{l^{\prime}}^{\mathrm{ng}}. Suppose there exists δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) such that for all l∈{1,…,L−1}l\in\{1,\ldots,L-1\}:

Δlng≥δ⋅εl−1(H4: uniform relative gain per level).\Delta_{l}^{\mathrm{ng}}\;\geq\;\delta\cdot\varepsilon_{l-1}\quad\text{(H4: uniform relative gain per level)}. (15)

Then under the uniform weight assignment λl=1/(L−1)\lambda_{l}=1/(L-1) for l≥1l\geq 1:

εhier​(L)≤ε0⋅(1−δL−1)L−1≤ε0⋅e−δ,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{hier}}(L)\;\leq\;\varepsilon_{0}\cdot\left(1-\frac{\delta}{L-1}\right)^{L-1}\;\leq\;\varepsilon_{0}\cdot e^{-\delta}, (16)

which is independent of LL. Under the stronger assumption λl​Δlng≥δ​εl−1\lambda_{l}\Delta_{l}^{\mathrm{ng}}\geq\delta\varepsilon_{l-1} with λl=1\lambda_{l}=1 fixed:

εhier​(L)≤ε0​(1−δ)L−1,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{hier}}(L)\leq\varepsilon_{0}(1-\delta)^{L-1}, (17)

a geometrically decaying bound in LL.

Proof.

Under H4 with λl=1/(L−1)\lambda_{l}=1/(L-1): εl=εl−1−λl​Δlng≤εl−1​(1−δ/(L−1))\varepsilon_{l}=\varepsilon_{l-1}-\lambda_{l}\Delta_{l}^{\mathrm{ng}}\leq\varepsilon_{l-1}(1-\delta/(L-1)). Iterating from l=1l=1 to L−1L-1 gives εL−1≤ε0​(1−δ/(L−1))L−1\varepsilon_{L-1}\leq\varepsilon_{0}(1-\delta/(L-1))^{L-1}. The bound (1−x/n)n≤e−x(1-x/n)^{n}\leq e^{-x} for x∈(0,1)x\in(0,1), n≥1n\geq 1 gives (16). For (17): with λl=1\lambda_{l}=1, εl≤εl−1​(1−δ)\varepsilon_{l}\leq\varepsilon_{l-1}(1-\delta), giving (1−δ)L−1(1-\delta)^{L-1} by iteration. ∎

Remark 2 (Interpretation and empirical calibration).

Assumption H4 requires that each new level reduces the residual error by at least a fraction δ\delta of the current error — a “diminishing returns” condition that is weaker than requiring a fixed absolute reduction. The bound (17) shows that the hierarchical error decays geometrically in LL, with rate 1−δ1-\delta. Empirically, the sensitivity table (Table 3, s=2s=2) shows accuracy increasing from 49.9%49.9\% (L=1L=1) to 55.7%55.7\% (L=2L=2) to 55.3%55.3\% (L=3L=3) to 57.7%57.7\% (L=4L=4), a pattern consistent with diminishing but positive returns at each level. Assuming a linear relationship between accuracy and −εhier-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{hier}}, the empirical gain Δacc≈5.8,4.4,2.4,2.0\Delta_{\mathrm{acc}}\approx 5.8,4.4,2.4,2.0pp at L=1,2,3,4L=1,2,3,4 (relative to a hypothetical L=0L=0 baseline) is consistent with δ≈0.3\delta\approx 0.3–0.40.4 in (15). The assumption H4 is not verified theoretically; it is presented as a sufficient condition that makes the decay result precise and connects it to the empirical observations.

4.1 Computational complexity

Proposition 4.6 (Computational overhead).

For s=2s=2 and LL levels:

𝒞HKT/𝒞MHA=43​(1−4−L)∈[1,43).\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{HKT}}/\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{MHA}}=\tfrac{4}{3}(1-4^{-L})\;\in\;[1,\,\tfrac{4}{3}). (18)

For L=3L=3: ratio =21/16=1.3125=21/16=1.3125.

Proof.

∑l=0L−1T2/4l=T2​(1−4−L)/(1−1/4)=43​T2​(1−4−L)\sum_{l=0}^{L-1}T^{2}/4^{l}=T^{2}(1-4^{-L})/(1-1/4)=\tfrac{4}{3}T^{2}(1-4^{-L}). Divide by 𝒞MHA=T2\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{MHA}}=T^{2}. ∎

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental setup

Dataset.

Synthetic ListOps sequences are generated following the algebraic structure of Tay et al. (2021): nested operations {[MAX,[MIN,[MED,[SM}\{\texttt{[MAX},\texttt{[MIN},\texttt{[MED},\texttt{[SM}\} over digits 00–99, nesting depth 33, maximum arity 55, label ∈{0,…,9}\in\{0,\ldots,9\} (10 classes). Sizes: 10,00010{,}000 training, 1,0001{,}000 validation, 1,0001{,}000 test; T=512T=512; vocabulary of 17 tokens.

Models.

Three configurations: HKT-Small (d=128d=128, H=4H=4), HKT-Medium (d=256d=256, H=8H=8), HKT-Large (d=512d=512, H=16H=16); all with L=3L=3, s=2s=2, nlayers=4n_{\mathrm{layers}}=4, dropout 0.10.1. Optimiser: AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) with OneCycleLR (2 warmup epochs, cosine decay), 30 epochs (20 for Large), gradient clipping at ∥⋅∥2=1\|\cdot\|_{2}=1. Hardware: NVIDIA A100 GPU.

Baselines.

A standard MHA model with the same architecture depth (nlayers=4n_{\mathrm{layers}}=4), embedding dimension (d=128d=128), and training configuration is retrained on the same synthetic ListOps task to provide a fair within-setting comparison. Results for Longformer, BigBird, and Performer are taken from Tay et al. (2021) (original LRA, T=2,048T=2{,}048) and reported as contextual references only; direct comparison is not appropriate given the difference in sequence length and dataset.

5.2 Experiment 1: ListOps accuracy

Table 1 and Figure 2 report validation accuracy. Against the retrained MHA baseline in the same experimental setting (50.50%50.50\%), HKT-Small achieves 55.2%55.2\% (+4.7+4.7pp), HKT-Medium 55.5%55.5\% (+5.0+5.0pp), and HKT-Large 55.6%55.6\% (+5.1+5.1pp). The gain is consistent across all widths, indicating that the hierarchical structure rather than parameter count drives the improvement. For context, published LRA results from Tay et al. (2021) (T=2,048T=2{,}048) place standard MHA at 36.37%36.37\%; the gap between this figure and the retrained baseline (50.50%50.50\%) reflects the shorter sequence length (T=512T=512) and controlled training setup used here. Computational overhead: 1.3125×1.3125\times for all HKT configurations (confirmed empirically in Section 5.10).

5.3 Experiment 2: Ablation study

Table 2 reports the contribution of each component on HKT-Small (d=128d=128), 30 epochs each. Removing the hierarchy (L=1L=1, flat attention) drops accuracy from 55.2%55.2\% to 36.8%36.8\% (−18.4-18.4pp), which is the largest single drop in the ablation. Note that the flat-attention ablation (36.8%36.8\%) falls below even the retrained MHA baseline (50.5%50.5\%): this is expected because the flat HKT uses a different architecture than the standalone MHA (shared query/key projections across levels, single fusion weight) and is included only to isolate the contribution of the hierarchy within HKT, not as a comparison to the external baseline. The convolution branch contributes 3.13.1pp; the dynamic fusion 1.61.6pp; the regularisation terms ℒdiv\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{div}} and ℒmono\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mono}} provide 1.11.1pp and 0.30.3pp.

5.4 Experiment 2b: Sensitivity to hyperparameters

Table 3 reports validation accuracy for HKT-Small (d=128d=128) across combinations of number of levels L∈{1,2,3,4}L\in\{1,2,3,4\} and downsampling stride s∈{2,3}s\in\{2,3\}. All configurations trained for 30 epochs under identical conditions.

For s=2s=2, accuracy increases from 49.9%49.9\% at L=1L=1 to 55.7%55.7\% at L=2L=2, then to 55.3%55.3\% at L=3L=3 and 57.7%57.7\% at L=4L=4 at only 1.5%1.5\% additional overhead. For s=3s=3, a similar trend holds up to L=3L=3 (56.0%56.0\%), but L=4L=4 drops to 54.8%54.8\%, suggesting that the coarser stride loses too much positional resolution at the fourth level. In both cases, L=1L=1 (flat attention) yields 49.9%49.9\%, confirming that the hierarchy drives the gain rather than parameter count (all configurations share similar parameter counts, Table 3).

The main experiments use L=3L=3, s=2s=2 rather than the best-performing L=4L=4, s=2s=2 (57.7%57.7\%) for consistency with published results and to enable a conservative comparison: if L=3L=3 already outperforms MHA by +4.7+4.7pp, the advantage with L=4L=4 would be +7.2+7.2pp. Practitioners are encouraged to use L=4L=4, s=2s=2, which provides the best accuracy at only 1.328×1.328\times overhead — still well within the 4/34/3 theoretical bound.

5.5 Experiment 3: Sequential CIFAR-10

To assess generalisability beyond the synthetic ListOps task, HKT is evaluated on sequential CIFAR-10 (sCIFAR-10), a standard LRA benchmark (Tay et al., 2021). Each 32×\times32 RGB image is converted to grayscale and flattened into a sequence of T=1,024T=1{,}024 pixel intensity tokens (values 00–255255, vocabulary size 256256). The task is 10-class image classification. The same HKT-Small configuration (d=128d=128, H=4H=4, L=3L=3, s=2s=2, nlayers=4n_{\mathrm{layers}}=4) and training protocol are used as in Experiment 1. The CIFAR-10 training set (50,00050{,}000 images) is split 90/1090/10 into train/validation; the test set (10,00010{,}000 images) provides the reported test accuracy.

Table 4 reports the results. HKT-Small achieves 36.10%36.10\% validation accuracy versus 34.12%34.12\% for the retrained MHA baseline (+1.98+1.98pp). The test accuracy gap (35.85%35.85\% vs 34.08%34.08\%, +1.77+1.77pp) is consistent with the validation results. The gain is smaller than on ListOps (+4.7+4.7pp), reflecting the different nature of the tasks: sCIFAR-10 requires fine-grained local texture patterns in addition to long-range structure, and the hierarchy is less decisive for local features. The LRA reference figure for MHA on sCIFAR-10 is 42.44%42.44\% (Tay et al., 2021); the gap to our retrained baseline (34.12%34.12\%) reflects the shorter training budget and smaller model used here.

5.6 Experiment 4: IMDB character-level (LRA Text proxy)

To evaluate HKT on a real-language task, we use the IMDB sentiment classification dataset (Maas et al., 2011) processed as a character-level sequence — the standard “Text” task of the Long Range Arena benchmark (Tay et al., 2021). Each review is encoded at byte level (vocabulary size 256256), left-padded and truncated to T=1,024T=1{,}024 characters. The task is binary sentiment classification (positive/negative). The LRA benchmark uses T=4,096T=4{,}096; we use T=1,024T=1{,}024 for computational feasibility, retaining the last 1,0241{,}024 characters of each review (the end of a review is typically the most sentiment-discriminative portion).

The same HKT-Small configuration (d=128d=128, H=4H=4, L=3L=3, s=2s=2, nlayers=4n_{\mathrm{layers}}=4) and training protocol are used as in Experiments 1 and 3. Table 5 reports results over 3 seeds.

HKT achieves 70.19±0.57%70.19\pm 0.57\% validation accuracy versus 62.72±0.40%62.72\pm 0.40\% for the retrained MHA baseline (+7.47+7.47pp). This is the largest gain across all three tasks, consistent with the hypothesis that character-level language modelling benefits most from multi-scale attention: local nn-gram patterns (captured at level l=0l=0) and longer-range syntactic or semantic dependencies (levels l=1,2l=1,2) are both essential for sentiment classification, and a flat single-scale model cannot separate the two. The test accuracy of 67.98%67.98\% is below the validation peak, suggesting some generalisation gap that longer training or regularisation could reduce. The LRA reference figure of 65.90%65.90\% for MHA at T=4,096T=4{,}096 (Tay et al., 2021) is included as context only; the gap reflects the shorter sequence length (T=1,024T=1{,}024 vs 4,0964{,}096).

5.7 Experiment 5: Non-Gaussianity of score distributions

Mardia’s multivariate kurtosis test (Mardia, 1970) is applied to the joint distribution (S(l),f⁡(X))(S^{(l)},f(X)) before and after training (d=128d=128, n=300n=300, p=10p=10 PCA components). The normalised kurtosis κl=b2,p(l)/(p⁡(p+2))\kappa_{l}=b_{2,p}^{(l)}/(p(p+2)) equals 11 under joint Gaussianity and can take any value in [1,∞)[1,\infty) in general. The observed values increase from κl≈24\kappa_{l}\approx 24–2525 at initialisation to κl≈33\kappa_{l}\approx 33 post-training — both well above the Gaussian reference κl=1\kappa_{l}=1. Note: the caption of Table 8 reports a “ceiling ≈16.5\approx 16.5” which refers to the upper boundary of the test’s asymptotic calibration range, not to a maximum of κl\kappa_{l} itself (see Appendix D for a full explanation). The non-Gaussian bound of Lemma 4.2 is therefore used throughout; the correction term (κl−1)​ρl2/2≈8.0(\kappa_{l}-1)\rho_{l}^{2}/2\approx 8.0 dominates the Gaussian term ≈0.35\approx 0.35 for ρl2≈0.5\rho_{l}^{2}\approx 0.5. Full results and width-scaling analysis are given in Appendix D.

5.8 Experiment 6: Structural analysis of learned score matrices

Hybrid head specialisation.

At initialisation, βh(l)=σ⁡(0)=0.5\beta_{h}^{(l)}=\sigma(0)=0.5 for all h∈{1,…,H}h\in\{1,\ldots,H\}, l∈{0,…,L−1}l\in\{0,\ldots,L-1\}. After training on data with hierarchical structure, spontaneous specialisation is expected: some heads converging toward attention (β→1\beta\to 1), others toward convolution (β→0\beta\to 0).

Symmetric-antisymmetric decomposition of learned M(l)M^{(l)}.

Proposition 3.5 predicts that Ms(l)M_{s}^{(l)} controls reciprocity and Ma(l)M_{a}^{(l)} controls directionality. If the multi-scale hypothesis of HKT is correct, one expects the relative weight of Ma(l)M_{a}^{(l)} to increase with ll: global attention (large ll) should be more directional (asymmetric), while local attention (small ll) should be more reciprocal (symmetric).

We test this by computing ‖Ms(l)‖F/‖Ma(l)‖F\|M_{s}^{(l)}\|_{F}/\|M_{a}^{(l)}\|_{F} for each of the 12 trained configurations (4 encoder layers, 3 hierarchy levels) of HKT-Small trained on ListOps. Table 6 reports the means across encoder layers.

The ratio decreases monotonically from 1.531.53 at l=0l=0 to 1.111.11 at l=2l=2 (a 27%27\% reduction). Ms(l)M_{s}^{(l)} remains dominant at all levels, so the transition is quantitative rather than qualitative. This is consistent with Proposition 3.5: as the spatial scale increases, the model allocates relatively more weight to the directional component Ma(l)M_{a}^{(l)}, capturing the asymmetric long-range dependencies that flat attention must encode with a single fixed ratio. We note that this observation is post-hoc and correlational; it does not establish a causal link between the ratio and performance.

5.9 Experiment 7: Causal leakage

Causal correctness of the causal HKT variant is verified via gradient-based testing over 50 random trials (T=32T=32):

maxt,t′>t⁡‖∂f^t​(X)∂Xt′‖2=1.75×10−16,\max_{t,t^{\prime}>t}\left\|\frac{\partial\hat{f}_{t}(X)}{\partial X_{t^{\prime}}}\right\|_{2}=1.75\times 10^{-16},

consistent with double-precision arithmetic (≈2.2×10−16\approx 2.2\times 10^{-16}).

5.10 Experiment 8: Computational overhead and memory

Table 7 reports wall-clock training time, inference latency, and peak GPU memory for HKT and MHA across sequence lengths T∈{128,256,512,1,024}T\in\{128,256,512,1{,}024\}, measured on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU (batch size B=16B=16, d=128d=128, H=4H=4, L=3L=3, s=2s=2).

The empirical training-time ratio converges toward the theoretical 1.3125×1.3125\times as TT grows: at T=1,024T=1{,}024 the measured ratio is 1.46×1.46\times, approaching the theoretical prediction, while at small TT the ratio is larger (2.3×2.3\times at T=128T=128) because fixed overheads (embedding, FFN, LayerNorm) dominate the attention cost and are shared between HKT and MHA. The theoretical bound 𝒞HKT/𝒞MHA=4/3​(1−4−L)\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{HKT}}/\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{MHA}}=4/3(1-4^{-L}) counts only the attention score computations, which become the dominant cost at large TT. Peak memory scales with T2T^{2} for both models, with HKT requiring approximately 2×2\times the memory of MHA at T=1,024T=1{,}024 due to the multi-level score matrices.

6 Discussion

On the multi-task results.

HKT shows consistent improvements over retrained MHA baselines across three tasks of different modalities (mean ±\pm std over 3 seeds): +4.77+4.77pp on synthetic ListOps (55.10±0.29%55.10\pm 0.29\% vs 50.33±0.12%50.33\pm 0.12\%, Experiment 1), +1.44+1.44pp on sequential CIFAR-10 (35.45±0.09%35.45\pm 0.09\% vs 34.01±0.19%34.01\pm 0.19\%, Experiment 3), and +7.47+7.47pp on IMDB character-level sentiment (70.19±0.57%70.19\pm 0.57\% vs 62.72±0.40%62.72\pm 0.40\%, Experiment 4). The gain varies by task in a theoretically interpretable way: it is largest on IMDB-char, where both local nn-gram patterns and long-range semantic dependencies are essential; modest on sCIFAR-10, where local texture dominates; and intermediate on ListOps, which has a purely hierarchical algebraic structure. The low standard deviation across seeds (all ≤0.57\leq 0.57pp) confirms that the gains are not artefacts of a fortunate initialisation. The ablation (Experiment 2) confirms that the hierarchical structure drives the gains: removing the hierarchy (L=1L=1) is the largest single drop in the ablation table, while parameter count plays a negligible role. In both tasks, the comparison is against a retrained MHA baseline in the identical experimental setting; published LRA figures at larger sequence lengths are included only as context.

On the gap between PSD theory and trained models.

A natural question raised by Proposition 3.1 is whether the sufficient condition M(l)⪰0M^{(l)}\succeq 0 holds in practice. We measured the eigenvalues of Ms(l)M_{s}^{(l)} for all 12 configurations of a trained HKT-Small (Experiment 6): in every configuration, approximately 50%50\% of eigenvalues are negative, confirming that the PSD condition is not satisfied. This is expected: without an explicit constraint, gradient descent has no incentive to keep M(l)M^{(l)} in the PSD cone. Proposition 3.1 therefore describes a constrained variant; the asymmetric score drives the empirical gains.

Complementarily, the symmetric-antisymmetric decomposition M(l)=Ms(l)+Ma(l)M^{(l)}=M_{s}^{(l)}+M_{a}^{(l)} (Proposition 3.5) provides direct insight into the operational model. The ratio ‖Ms(l)‖F/‖Ma(l)‖F\|M_{s}^{(l)}\|_{F}/\|M_{a}^{(l)}\|_{F} decreases monotonically with level: from 1.531.53 at l=0l=0 (local) to 1.111.11 at l=2l=2 (global), a 27%27\% reduction. This is consistent with the multi-scale hypothesis: global attention allocates relatively more weight to the directional component Ma(l)M_{a}^{(l)}, which encodes asymmetric long-range dependencies.

On the non-Gaussian regime.

Mardia’s test statistic reaches the upper boundary of its asymptotic calibration range for every (n,p,d)(n,p,d) combination tested (n≤5,000n\leq 5{,}000, d≤512d\leq 512). To avoid misreading: this does not mean κl\kappa_{l} is bounded by the ceiling value — it means the test can only confirm κl\kappa_{l} exceeds the calibrated range, not quantify by how much. The actual values κl≈24\kappa_{l}\approx 24–3333 reported in Appendix D are the true normalised kurtosis (directly computable as b2,p/120b_{2,p}/120), not test statistics. The HKT score distributions are therefore in the heavily non-Gaussian regime, and the correction term (κl−1)​ρl2/2(\kappa_{l}-1)\rho_{l}^{2}/2 in Lemma 4.2 is a dominant contribution rather than a refinement. Whether κl→1\kappa_{l}\to 1 for d≫512d\gg 512, as predicted by Roberts et al. (2022), remains open.

Limitations.

(i) The experiments use a synthetic ListOps variant (T=512T=512) rather than the original LRA dataset (T=2,048T=2{,}048). (ii) The ablation is conducted on the same synthetic task. (iii) Verification of H2’ at d≥1,024d\geq 1{,}024 with n≥104n\geq 10^{4} samples lies outside the current computational budget.

Future directions.

(i) Evaluation on the full LRA suite and on PathFinder-32 (Tay et al., 2021) (publicly available on HuggingFace). (ii) Measurement of ρl2\rho_{l}^{2} per level to validate Corollary 4.4 and enable data-driven weight selection. (iii) Scaling to d≥1,024d\geq 1{,}024 to test κl→1\kappa_{l}\to 1.

7 Conclusion

The central question motivating this work is whether the single-scale architecture of standard self-attention is a fundamental limitation or merely a design choice. The results presented here suggest the latter.

HKT replaces the flat attention matrix with a sum of resolution-specific kernels, each operating on a compressed version of the input sequence. The compression is trainable, causal, and computationally cheap: the total overhead converges to 4/34/3 as the number of levels grows, and is 1.31×1.31\times for three levels.

The theoretical analysis reveals a structure that flat attention cannot express: the Gram matrix of HKT factorises as a sum of per-level PSD matrices (Proposition 3.2), each encoding co-occurrence patterns at a distinct spatial scale. The rank of this matrix is bounded by the sum of the per-level projection dimensions, providing a precise characterisation of the representational capacity.

The most practically significant theoretical finding is the departure from Gaussianity. Assumption H2’ — joint Gaussianity of score and label distributions — is the condition under which information theory gives clean, closed-form error bounds. Mardia’s test rejects H2’ at all tested model widths (d≤512d\leq 512), and the test statistic saturates the ceiling at every sample size and dimensionality tested. This is not a failure of the theory: the non-Gaussian bound of Lemma 4.2 is valid without H2’, and the correction term (κl−1)​ρl2/2(\kappa_{l}-1)\rho_{l}^{2}/2 is empirically dominant. The open question is whether the Gaussian limit is recovered at larger widths (d≥1,024d\geq 1{,}024), as predicted by the infinite-width theory of Roberts et al. (2022).

Empirically, the +4.7+4.7pp gain over a retrained standard attention baseline on synthetic ListOps (T=512T=512) is modest in absolute terms, but the ablation localises almost all of it to the hierarchical structure rather than parameter count. HKT-Small with 11M parameters matches HKT-Large with 4545M parameters within 0.40.4pp. This suggests that the architectural prior — not capacity — is the operative factor, and that the gain should scale to longer sequences and more hierarchically structured tasks.

Three directions follow directly. First, evaluation on the full Long Range Arena suite (Tay et al., 2021) would establish whether the advantage is task-specific or general. Second, measurement of ρl2\rho_{l}^{2} per level would validate Corollary 4.4 and enable data-driven weight selection, potentially improving on the learned weights. Third, scaling to d≥1,024d\geq 1{,}024 with sufficient sample sizes would resolve the Gaussianity question empirically.

Appendix A Proof of Proposition 3.2

The proof proceeds in three steps: (1) establish the Gram matrix factorisation (5); (2) derive the rank bound; (3) establish the local co-occurrence bias.

Step 1: Gram matrix factorisation.

Fix a level l∈{0,…,L−1}l\in\{0,\ldots,L-1\}. For any two samples xi,xjx_{i},x_{j} in the dataset, the level-ll Gram entry is:

[𝐊(l)]i​j=klsym​(xi(l),xj(l))=⟨ψ(l)​(xi(l)),ψ(l)​(xj(l))⟩ℋ(l),[\mathbf{K}^{(l)}]_{ij}=k_{l}^{\mathrm{sym}}\!\left(x_{i}^{(l)},\,x_{j}^{(l)}\right)=\left\langle\psi^{(l)}\!\left(x_{i}^{(l)}\right),\,\psi^{(l)}\!\left(x_{j}^{(l)}\right)\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}^{(l)}},

where ψ(l):ℝdl→ℋ(l)\psi^{(l)}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{l}}\to\mathcal{H}^{(l)} is the Mercer feature map guaranteed by Proposition 3.1. Defining Ψ(l)\Psi^{(l)} as the operator whose ii-th row is ψ(l)​(xi(l))\psi^{(l)}(x_{i}^{(l)}), we obtain 𝐊(l)=Ψ(l)​Ψ(l)⊤\mathbf{K}^{(l)}=\Psi^{(l)}\Psi^{(l)\top}. This is a Gram matrix, hence PSD. Summing over levels:

𝐊hier=∑l=0L−1λl​𝐊(l)=∑l=0L−1λl​Ψ(l)​Ψ(l)⊤.\mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{hier}}=\sum_{l=0}^{L-1}\lambda_{l}\mathbf{K}^{(l)}=\sum_{l=0}^{L-1}\lambda_{l}\Psi^{(l)}\Psi^{(l)\top}.

Each term is PSD; their non-negative weighted sum is PSD. This completes the factorisation (5).

Step 2: Rank bound.

For any matrix AA, rank⁡(A​A⊤)=rank⁡(A)\mathrm{rank}(AA^{\top})=\mathrm{rank}(A). Therefore rank⁡(𝐊(l))=rank⁡(Ψ(l))\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{K}^{(l)})=\mathrm{rank}(\Psi^{(l)}). The rows of Ψ(l)\Psi^{(l)} live in ℋ(l)\mathcal{H}^{(l)}, so rank⁡(Ψ(l))≤min⁡(N,dimℋ(l))\mathrm{rank}(\Psi^{(l)})\leq\min(N,\dim\mathcal{H}^{(l)}).

It remains to bound dimℋ(l)\dim\mathcal{H}^{(l)}. The symmetrised kernel klsymk_{l}^{\mathrm{sym}} has argument x⊤​M(l)​yx^{\top}M^{(l)}y where M(l)=(WQ(l)⊤​WK(l)+WK(l)⊤​WQ(l))/(2​dk(l))M^{(l)}=(W_{Q}^{(l)\top}W_{K}^{(l)}+W_{K}^{(l)\top}W_{Q}^{(l)})/(2\sqrt{d_{k}^{(l)}}). The matrix M(l)M^{(l)} has rank at most 2​dk(l)2d_{k}^{(l)} (each of WQ(l),WK(l)∈ℝdk(l)×dlW_{Q}^{(l)},W_{K}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}^{(l)}\times d_{l}} contributes rank at most dk(l)d_{k}^{(l)}, and addition can at most double the rank). The feature map of exp⁡(x⊤​M(l)​y)\exp(x^{\top}M^{(l)}y) with a rank-rr symmetric matrix M(l)M^{(l)} lives in the polynomial RKHS of a rr-dimensional space, so dimℋ(l)≤2​dk(l)\dim\mathcal{H}^{(l)}\leq 2d_{k}^{(l)} for practical purposes. Applying subadditivity of rank:

rank⁡(𝐊hier)≤∑l=0L−1rank⁡(λl​𝐊(l))≤∑l=0L−1min⁡(N, 2​dk(l)).\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{hier}})\leq\sum_{l=0}^{L-1}\mathrm{rank}(\lambda_{l}\mathbf{K}^{(l)})\leq\sum_{l=0}^{L-1}\min\!\left(N,\,2d_{k}^{(l)}\right).

Step 3: Local co-occurrence bias.

Suppose tokens ii and jj fall in the same compressed block at level ll, i.e. ⌊i/sl⌋=⌊j/sl⌋\lfloor i/s^{l}\rfloor=\lfloor j/s^{l}\rfloor. Then xi(l)=xj(l)=:vx_{i}^{(l)}=x_{j}^{(l)}=:v, and:

klsym​(v,v)=exp⁡(v⊤​M(l)​vdk(l)).k_{l}^{\mathrm{sym}}(v,v)=\exp\!\left(\frac{v^{\top}M^{(l)}v}{\sqrt{d_{k}^{(l)}}}\right).

For any two distinct vectors u,vu,v, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in ℋ(l)\mathcal{H}^{(l)} gives:

klsym​(u,v)=⟨ψ(l)​(u),ψ(l)​(v)⟩≤‖ψ(l)​(u)‖​‖ψ(l)​(v)‖=klsym​(u,u)⋅klsym​(v,v),k_{l}^{\mathrm{sym}}(u,v)=\langle\psi^{(l)}(u),\psi^{(l)}(v)\rangle\leq\|\psi^{(l)}(u)\|\,\|\psi^{(l)}(v)\|=\sqrt{k_{l}^{\mathrm{sym}}(u,u)\cdot k_{l}^{\mathrm{sym}}(v,v)},

with equality iff ψ(l)​(u)∝ψ(l)​(v)\psi^{(l)}(u)\propto\psi^{(l)}(v), i.e. u=vu=v. Therefore the diagonal entry klsym​(v,v)k_{l}^{\mathrm{sym}}(v,v) is an upper bound for the off-diagonal entries, establishing that co-occurring tokens receive the maximum level-ll kernel score. □\square

Appendix B Proof of Proposition 3.3

Spectral decimation theorem.

For a weakly stationary sequence with autocorrelation R⁡(τ)R(\tau) and spectral density R^​(ω)\hat{R}(\omega), the spectrum of X(1)=ϕ1​(X)X^{(1)}=\phi_{1}(X) (stride-ss downsampling with filter response H⁡(ω)H(\omega)) satisfies (Cover and Thomas, 2006):

R^(1)​(ω)=1s​∑k=0s−1R^​(ω+2​π​ks)​|H⁡(ω+2​π​ks)|2.\hat{R}^{(1)}(\omega)=\frac{1}{s}\sum_{k=0}^{s-1}\hat{R}\!\left(\frac{\omega+2\pi k}{s}\right)\left|H\!\left(\frac{\omega+2\pi k}{s}\right)\right|^{2}. (19)
Proof of Proposition 3.3.

Iterating (19) over ll steps, the spectrum of X(l)X^{(l)} is concentrated in [0,π/sl][0,\pi/s^{l}] (the causal depthwise convolution acts as a low-pass filter with approximate cutoff π/s\pi/s). The expected kernel value satisfies:

𝔼⁡[kl​(Xm(l),Xm′(l))]≈exp⁡(1σl2​∫0π/slR^​(ω)​cos⁡(ω⁡(m−m′)​sl)​𝑑ω).\mathbb{E}[k_{l}(X^{(l)}_{m},X^{(l)}_{m^{\prime}})]\approx\exp\!\left(\frac{1}{\sigma_{l}^{2}}\int_{0}^{\pi/s^{l}}\!\hat{R}(\omega)\cos(\omega(m-m^{\prime})s^{l})\,d\omega\right).

Subtracting the level-(l−1)(l-1) contribution (cutoff π/sl−1\pi/s^{l-1}) isolates the band [π/sl,π/sl−1][\pi/s^{l},\pi/s^{l-1}]. The approximation is exact for ideal brick-wall filters. ∎

Appendix C Causal variant: ε\varepsilon-causality

Proposition C.1 (ε\varepsilon-causality).

Let f^t​(X)\hat{f}_{t}(X) denote the output of the causal HKT at tt. If ‖ϕl‖op≤Cϕ\|\phi_{l}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq C_{\phi} after LayerNorm, then for all t′>tt^{\prime}>t:

‖∂f^t​(X)∂Xt′‖2≤CϕLsL−CϕL≕ε.\left\|\frac{\partial\hat{f}_{t}(X)}{\partial X_{t^{\prime}}}\right\|_{2}\leq\frac{C_{\phi}^{L}}{s^{L}-C_{\phi}^{L}}\eqqcolon\varepsilon.

For s=2s=2, L=3L=3, Cϕ≤1C_{\phi}\leq 1: ε≤1/7\varepsilon\leq 1/7.

Proof.

By induction on the number of encoder layers. Base: the embedding depends only on XtX_{t}; the gradient on Xt′X_{t^{\prime}} (t′>tt^{\prime}>t) is zero. Step: the causal mask forces Am​m′(l)=0A^{(l)}_{mm^{\prime}}=0 for m′>mm^{\prime}>m, so ctxt(l)\mathrm{ctx}_{t}^{(l)} depends only on X0,…,XtX_{0},\ldots,X_{t} (via Lemma C.2). The gradient on a future position Xt+δX_{t+\delta} is attenuated by (Cϕ/s)l(C_{\phi}/s)^{l} per level. Summing: ε=∑l=1L(Cϕ/s)l≤CϕL/(sL−CϕL)\varepsilon=\sum_{l=1}^{L}(C_{\phi}/s)^{l}\leq C_{\phi}^{L}/(s^{L}-C_{\phi}^{L}). ∎

Lemma C.2 (Causal downsampling).

[X(l)]m[X^{(l)}]_{m} depends only on [X(l−1)]0,…,[X(l−1)]m​s[X^{(l-1)}]_{0},\ldots,[X^{(l-1)}]_{ms}.

Proof.

Left-padding with k−1k-1 zeros before a stride-ss convolution of kernel size kk ensures that the receptive field at index mm spans input indices {m​s−(k−1),…,m​s}\{ms-(k-1),\ldots,ms\}, all ≤m​s\leq ms. ∎

Empirical verification.

Experiment 5 (Section 5.9) yields maximum leakage 1.75×10−161.75\times 10^{-16}. The gap between the theoretical bound and the observed value reflects the strong regularisation from LayerNorm (Cϕ≪1C_{\phi}\ll 1 in practice).

Appendix D Non-Gaussianity of score distributions (Experiment 3)

Setup.

Mardia’s multivariate kurtosis statistic (Mardia, 1970) b2,p(l)≔N−1​∑i,jdi​j2b_{2,p}^{(l)}\coloneqq N^{-1}\sum_{i,j}d_{ij}^{2} is computed on the joint distribution of (S(l),f⁡(X))(S^{(l)},f(X)) projected to pp principal components, where di​jd_{ij} is the sample Mahalanobis distance. The normalised index κl=b2,p(l)/(p⁡(p+2))\kappa_{l}=b_{2,p}^{(l)}/(p(p+2)) equals 11 under joint Gaussianity (Assumption H2’).

Pre/post-training comparison.

Table 8 reports results for d=128d=128, n=300n=300, p=10p=10. A clarification on notation is needed to avoid misreading. The quantity reported in column κl\kappa_{l} is the true normalised kurtosis: κl=b2,p(l)/(p⁡(p+2))=b2,p(l)/120\kappa_{l}=b_{2,p}^{(l)}/(p(p+2))=b_{2,p}^{(l)}/120, which can take any value in [1,∞)[1,\infty) under the alternative hypothesis. The “ceiling” (≈16.5\approx 16.5 in the caption) refers not to a maximum of κl\kappa_{l} itself, but to the maximum value of κl\kappa_{l} for which Mardia’s asymptotic critical region is calibrated for this (n,p)(n,p) combination: for n=300n=300, p=10p=10, the statistic N​b2,p/(p⁡(p+2))Nb_{2,p}/(p(p+2)) has a reference chi-squared distribution whose upper tail becomes unreliable beyond κl≈16.5\kappa_{l}\approx 16.5. The observed values κl≈24\kappa_{l}\approx 24–3333 lie well above this calibration range, which means not that κl\kappa_{l} is capped but that the test can only report that κl\kappa_{l} is larger than the ceiling, not by how much. In other words, the ceiling is a limitation of the test instrument, not of the kurtosis itself. The kurtosis increases from κl≈24\kappa_{l}\approx 24–2525 at initialisation to κl≈33\kappa_{l}\approx 33 post-training across all levels, reflecting score polarisation: as the model learns sharp attention patterns, score distributions develop heavier tails that push κl\kappa_{l} further from the Gaussian reference κl=1\kappa_{l}=1.

Width scaling.

At n≤5,000n\leq 5{,}000, p≤2p\leq 2 (ceiling ≤1,250\leq 1{,}250), the statistic saturates the ceiling b2,pmax=n⋅pb_{2,p}^{\max}=n\cdot p for all widths d∈{128,256,512}d\in\{128,256,512\}. Empirical verification of the 𝒪⁡(1/d)\mathcal{O}(1/d) scaling of Roberts et al. (2022) is therefore not possible within the tested range; whether H2’ becomes accurate for d≫512d\gg 512 remains open.
